summary: Modifies the device-independent graphics display proposal in RFC 177. The main change is how coordinate areas on the network standard graphics screen are defined, to avoid a problem found with the earlier definition and to be more flexible.

eli5.summary: The first picture-describing plan had a problem with how it marked off areas on the screen. This note changes the rules so they work better.

questions: how are graphics coordinate areas defined
what is the network standard graphics screen
what did rfc 181 change in rfc 177
subtitle: A revision to how coordinate areas work in the network standard graphics display list proposal.

tldr.problem: In the graphics proposal of RFC 177, areas of the network standard graphics screen were meant to be absolute boundaries but could be crossed by an executing list, and scaling was awkward.
tldr.mechanism: Coordinates become 16-bit unsigned normalized fractions measured from the lower left corner of an area or image space, and EXECUTE LIST and COPY LIST take two corner points that define the image area.
tldr.outcome: This lets each list be scaled differently on each execution. It also adds mode stacks and changes DEFINE LIST. It updates RFC 177.

today: RFC 181 updates RFC 177. The metadata lists its status as Unknown and no later RFC as replacing it.

sections.title: The Problem with RFC 177 Areas
sections.content: This RFC modifies the proposal for a device-independent graphical display description in RFC 177, using its terms. The earlier problem was that areas of the NGS (network standard graphics screen), meant to be absolute boundaries, could be crossed when a list ran inside them. Scaling of lists in the network standard graphic display list (NGDL) was also awkwardly done with specific commands.
sections.eli5: Pictures could spill out of their frames, and shrinking them was clumsy.

sections.title: Areas and Relative Coordinates
sections.content:
Coordinates stay 16-bit unsigned normalized fractions, leaving resolution to the receiving device. They are now fractional displacements from the lower left corner of the screen, an area or an image space.

Areas stay rectangular and may overlap but not completely contain another area. An area has a 16-bit integer name and two (x,y) pairs for its lower left and upper right corners with respect to the NGS. No list executed in an area may cross its boundaries.
sections.eli5: Positions are now measured as a fraction of the frame, so the same picture fits any frame size.

sections.title: Execute List, Scaling and Mode Stacks
sections.content:
List item types 7 and 8 change to EXECUTE LIST (Name,(Xl,Yl),(Xr,Yr)) and COPY LIST (Name,(Xl,Yl),(Xr,Yr)). The two pairs define the image area as displacements from the lower left corner of the containing area, so each list can be scaled differently each time and can even be distorted if the X and Y ratios differ. Tables (item type 9) are relative to the area valid when they run.

Executing a list saves the current state, computes a new origin, resets NGLP to zero and calculates new X and Y scale factors. A mode stack is added for each graphics mode, with PUSH CHARACTER MODE (14), PUSH VECTOR MODE (15), POP CHARACTER MODE (16) and POP VECTOR MODE (17).
sections.eli5: Each time you stick a picture into a frame you say how big, and the computer remembers your old pen settings so it can go back to them.

sections.title: Other Changes
sections.content: DEFINE LIST (type 1) now takes a 16-bit integer name and a 16-bit length in bytes rather than items. This eases processing and eliminates the TABLE item (type 11). The first three list items drop the WORD IMAGE, since they now define NGS areas, and DEFINE IMAGE ARE (type 2) becomes DEFINE AREA.
sections.eli5: A few commands get new names and simpler settings to make the rulebook tidier.

references.text: RFC 177, the device independent graphical display description proposal.
